speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic, I am Dr. Agent. You mentioned sudden-onset vertigo; to begin our assessment, have you experienced any severe headache, double vision, or difficulty speaking alongside the spinning sensation?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. Since the episode lasted only about three minutes and you are now back to baseline, this sounds like a transient event; did you notice any nystagmus (eye twitching), hearing loss, or tinnitus during the attack? Additionally, did you have any recent head trauma or a history of high blood pressure?

REQUEST TEST: Basic_Metabolic_Panel, Lipid_Profile, Homocysteine_Level
REQUEST IMAGES: None (pending further history)

speaker: Doctor
text:
The metabolic and lipid panels are normal, which is good. Given the brief duration of your vertigo and the absence of other neurological deficits, have you experienced any hearing changes, such as muffled hearing or ringing in your ears, during the episode?

REQUEST TEST: Audiometry; REQUEST TEST: Serum_Anti_GABA_B; REQUEST TEST: Serum_Anti_AQP4

speaker: Doctor
text: Since your audiometry and antibody tests are normal, ruling out Meniere's disease and autoimmune causes, have you experienced any recent severe stress, sleep deprivation, or consumption of alcohol or caffeine prior to this brief episode? Also, do you have a history of migraines, even if they rarely involved a headache?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The patient's symptoms of vertigo, nausea, and vomiting are concerning for a central cause given the sudden onset. To rule out a stroke, I need to know if you noticed any weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of your face or body during the episode. Also, did the spinning sensation occur spontaneously or was it triggered by a specific head movement?

REQUEST TEST: MRI_Brain_With_Diffusion

speaker: Doctor
text:
The normal MRI brain with diffusion is excellent news as it effectively rules out an acute ischemic stroke or hemorrhage. Given the duration of your symptoms (3 minutes) and the absence of focal neurological deficits, have you noticed any specific head movements, such as turning your head in bed or looking up, that triggered the spinning sensation?

REQUEST TEST: None pending final history.
REQUEST IMAGES: None requested as MRI is negative.

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on your normal MRI and the very brief duration of the episode, I am confident this is not a stroke. However, to confirm Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), I need to know exactly which head movements triggered the spinning sensation, as this will guide our physical examination.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

The brief, transient nature of your vertigo (lasting only 3 minutes), the absence of central neurological signs on your MRI, and your lack of hearing loss strongly point to BPPV. To confirm this, I need to know exactly what head movements triggered the spinning sensation, such as rolling over in bed or looking up.
